author: Jesse Campbell
title: Versatile Ashe economy evolves, comes together following pandemic and Helene - NewsBreak
text:
By Jesse Campbell ,
13 hours ago
ASHE COUNTY — “Mountain folks are masters at learning how to pivot,” said Ashe County Chamber of Commerce Executive Director Kitty Honeycutt on the local economy’s versatility following Hurricane Helene and the pandemic.
While the notorious historic storm shuttered thousands of businesses in western North Carolina, Ashe County shops and restaurants relied on persevering ingenuity and networking to weather the hurricane’s worst while finding steady ground in rapidly changing economic conditions.
The county’s robust visitor base also proved to be a welcoming panacea for the tourism industry, which sustained an untimely setback with the storm’s arrival before the peak leaf-looking season.
Volunteers and visitors help with economic rejuvenation
Although countless volunteers and rescue personnel ignored the travel advisories in bringing needed help and supplies to the county following the storm, tourism dollars provided another stimulating jolt to county businesses that would’ve suffered untold financial distress otherwise.
Those guests who were unable to wield chainsaws or pull dislodged drainage pipes and culverts from washed-out basins brought their wallets to help local businesses stay open.
“We had so many people here right after the storm,” said Honeycutt. “They were just here to help, and we were so grateful for that. We also had a lot of day trippers. People would say, ‘We just wanted to come and spend the day here to shop in stores.’ They wanted to help them (local businesses) to get back to the level they need and where they want to be.”
Although the storm’s closing of the Blue Ridge Parkway — a primary draw for regional visitors — brought fewer tourist dollars regionwide, Honeycutt said multi-day vacationers are returning to the High Country.
Good old-fashioned customer serviceAshe County businesses’ personal touch has proven to be an economic catalyst and advantage for niche markets, reapplying lessons learned during the pandemic when stay-at-home orders and travel advisories temporarily stymied the local economy.
“As I see it, the mom and pop small stores, the individual stores have done such a really great job of offering customer experience,” said Honeycutt. “While some of those Big Chain Stores also offer customer service and expertise, I think small stores and businesses have thought differently to engage customers and keep them loyal while enhancing their experience.”
While some stores have reverted to their pre-pandemic settings, Honeycutt said many local businesses have retained innovative customer interactions, such as online shopping and curbside pick-up, while adding new creative offerings and special events to lure customers.
“I’ve always been amazed at how inventive they (local businesses) can be,” said Honeycutt.
“All boats rise together”Although Laissez-faire market philosophies and dynamics can dictate cut-throat competition in other small communities fighting for the same dollar, Honeycutt said local merchants and restaurateurs are unique in how they refer customers to other local establishments while encouraging spending money across town.
Many local businesses also partner for cross-promotions and act as on-ad hoc travel guides, instructing guests on where to get a quick bite or grab the best deal on hiking boots from local outfitters, complementing their ideal mountain vacation.
Honeycutt said there’s “great handholding and collaboration” across multiple business sectors serving customers to complete the Ashe County vacation experience.
“All boats rise together,” said Honeycutt.
Lansing’s rebirthWhile some local businesses permanently closed after the storm, other developers have stepped in to reimagine damaged properties to assist the local economy.
Tim Cool, of Cool Enterprises LLC, recently purchased the former Country House Restaurant in Lansing with plans to renovate and lease the building to a new tenant, possibly another restaurant.
“Being able to purchase a part of downtown is a big deal for us,” said Cool. “We want to be part of the rebirth of Lansing post-Helene and for years to come.”
While several West Jefferson merchants have entered into an unspoken referral agreement to ensure tourism dollars are distributed proportionately throughout the business district, Lansing residents and business owners have also proudly displayed their community spirit by helping CJ’s Market reopen after Hurricane Helene.
The market officially reopened on Oct. 18.
“The cleanup process was rough; the volunteers and community did it,” said co-owner Trisha Hart about the store’s reopening. “It’s not something we did on our own. It was a community project. Everyone got their hands in there time and time again.”
